full_judgment: 15. In this regard, Mr. Shaukat Ali Khan, the learned Advocate, submits that non-examination and withholding of the rest of the witnesses mentioned in the charge-sheet gives rise to an adverse presumption under section 114(g) of the Evidence Act against the genuineness of the, prosecution case. In support of his such submission, the learned Advocate cited the decisions of the Supreme Court, High Court Division, in S.M. Farooque alias Syed Farooque Vs. The State reported in 28 DLRI92 and Ahmed Ali and another Vs. Haji Abdur Rashid and others reported in (1991) II BLD11. In the case reported in 28DLR192, there was an armed robbery committed in the house of one Dr. F. Hasan of Comilla town on 16.6.1978 at about 9-15 P.M. During the course of robbery, in the flash on electric tube light, the informant and other inmates of the house recognised the robbers and immediately after retreat of the; robbers the informant sent a telephone message to the Kotwali Police and on their advice lodged a written ejahar with the police station at 11-45 P.M. It as alleged on behalf of the defence in the said case that the telephone message and ejahar made at 11-45 P.M. did contain the story of recognition of the accused persons but was subsequently accommodated the earlier entries made in the General Diary on the next day only after their arrest on suspicion, by over-writings and interpolations. As such, the concerned Assistant Sub-Inspector of Police who received the telephone message and also the subsequent written ejahar ought to have been examined. It was held in that case that under section 114(g) of the Evidence Act, a presumption was drawn that had Mr. Malek been examined as a witness he would not have supported the prosecution case as to the time of filing the impugned first information report. In the case reported in XI BLD11, it was alleged that the accused made a confessional statement under section 164 of the Criminal Procedure Code and in pursuance of the said information along with some other police personnels recovered one gun and 19 cartridges and accordingly the case under section 19A and 19f of the Arms Act read with section 3 of the Special Powers Act was started. In that case it was contended on behalf of the accused that the prosecution did not produce the material and independent witnesses who were cited in the charge-sheet as witness to prove the prosecution case, as such, the trial Court ought to have drawn an adverse presumption against the genuineness of the case. In the said case also the high Court Division accepted the aforesaid contention and held that the witnesses named in the charge-sheet and alleged to have accompanied the informant in the place of occurrence and saw the alleged recovery of the arms and a munitions the non-examination of the said witnesses naturally gives rise to an advarse presumption against the genuineness of the prosecution case. This is no doubt the correct legal position and wisdom of these decisions are unquestionable. But the facts of the present case are different. In this case 13 persons were cited as witnesses and 7 of them were examined in Court as prosecution witnesses. But the rest of the persons do not posses any more knowledge spout the occurrence than what P.W.1 to 6 had already stated in their deposition. It should be borne in mind that it is for the prosecution to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt and, in view of section 134 of the Evidence Act, conviction can be based on the testimony even of a single witness if he is found to be reliable, unimpeachable and worthy of credit. Because the decision in a case depend on the quality of the testimony and not on the mere number of witnesses. In the instant case, the prosecution sought to prove its case, mainly on the basis of the evidence of PWs 1 to 6, regarding explosion, chase of the accused per-sons resulting in their arrest and recovery of a pipe gun. It is not suggested that a particular witness or witnesses, cited in the charge-sheet, had any special or exclusive knowledge about the above noted facts which are not known to the PWs 1 to 6 and withholding of such witnesses may give rise to an adverse presumption against genuineness of the prosecution case. An omnibus submission of the learned Advocate that non-examination of other witnesses cited in the charge-sheet, gives rise to suspicion about the genuineness of the prosecution case without imputing some relevant and specific knowledge on a particular witness or witnesses who was not examined, cannot be accepted as correct.
